topic.name: Differentiating an Inverse Function at a Point

question.text: Consider the function $f(x) =x^3 + e^x$ and the point $P(0,1)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(1,0).$
question.explanation:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,1).$

\begin{align*} f(x) &= x^3 + e^x \\ f'(x) &= 3x^2 + e^x \\ f'(0) &= 1 \end{align*}

Since $(0,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,0)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore, \begin{align} (f^{-1})'(1) &=\dfrac{1}{f'\left(f^{-1}\left(1\right) \right)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{f'(0)} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac 1 1\\[5pt] & = 1. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function

question.text: Consider the function $f(x) =1+2e^{x+1}.$ Given that $y = f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $(f^{-1})'(3).$
question.explanation:
To determine $(f^{-1})'(3),$ we use the following formula: \[ \left(f^{-1}\right)'(3) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(3))} \]

First, we calculate the value of $f^{-1}(3).$ To do this, we solve the equation $f^{-1}(3) = x.$ This gives \begin{align} f^{-1}(3) & = x\\[3pt] f(x) & = 3\\[3pt] 1+2e^{x+1}& = 3\\[3pt] 2e^{x+1}& = 2\\[3pt] e^{x+1}& = 1\\[3pt] x+1& = 0\\[3pt] x & =-1. \end{align}

Therefore, $f^{-1}(3) = -1.$

Now, we calculate $f'(-1),$ as follows: \begin{align} f(x) & = 1+2e^{x+1}\\[5pt] f'(x) &= 2 e^{x+1}\\[5pt] f'(-1) &= 2e^0\\[5pt] f'(-1) & = 2 \end{align}

Finally, we get \begin{align} \left(f^{-1}\right)'(3) & = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(3))}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{f'(-1)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align}

example.title: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions

question.text:
The following table gives the values of $f(x), f'(x),g(x),$ and $g'(x)$ at some points. Find $\left(g\cdot f^{-1}\right)'(3)$ of the product of functions.

$x$ $f(x)$ $f'(x)$ $g(x)$ $g'(x)$
$3$ $5$ $-2$ $-3$ $1$
$-2$ $3$ $-4$ $-2$ $-5$
question.explanation:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$ is \[ (f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}. \]

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function $g(x)f^{-1}(x)$ is \[ (g \cdot f^{-1})'(x)=g'(x)f^{-1}(x) + \dfrac{g(x)}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}. \]

Substituting $x=3,$ we have \[ (g\cdot f^{-1})'(3) =g'(3)f^{-1}(3) + \dfrac{g(3)}{f'(f^{-1}(3))}. \]

From the table, we obtain $f^{-1}(3)=-2,$ $g(3)=-3,$ $g'(3)=1,$ and $f'(-2)=-4.$ Therefore,

\begin{align*} (g\cdot f^{-1})'(3) &= g'(3)f^{-1}(3) + \dfrac{g(3)}{f'(f^{-1}(3))} \\[5pt] &= 1\cdot (-2) + \dfrac{-3}{f'(-2)} \\[5pt] &=-2+\dfrac{(-3)}{(-4)} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{5}{4}. \end{align*}
